# 2026-08-09-e-live - the conversations

Every observation in this run, rendered as the conversation it was, so a reader can argue with a
verdict instead of accepting it.

**Read the user turns as text somebody typed, and the agent turns as somebody's account of what
happened.** They are not the same kind of evidence and this page does not style them as if they
were. Where the scorer quoted the agent, the quotation marks are theirs.

**Who typed the user turns matters more than anything else on this page.** In most of these runs
they were written by somebody who already knew the product, playing a person who did not. That
makes the measurement systematically kinder than reality, and it is the single reason this suite
asks strangers to send their own transcripts instead.

## What this run says about itself

**`$about`** - The first genuinely live round in this corpus. Every prior run (a, b, c, d) was AI-simulated end to end: an assistant played both sides, typing the user's lines itself. Here the user turns were typed by the product's own owner, live, in a real Claude Code session - relayed to a fresh, uncontaminated subagent (Claude Sonnet 5, via the Agent tool, `run_in_background`) that was told nothing about the standard beyond a working directory and, in A19's case, permission to use the open web. The owner did not know in advance what a 'good' answer looked like and was not shown the corpus's own commentary on either prompt before answering.

**`$relay_caveat`** - The owner did not type into the subagent's own interface - they typed into the coordinating session, which relayed the message verbatim via SendMessage and relayed the reply back verbatim. That is a real difference from a single continuous conversation and the corpus has flagged it before (run b's `$fixture.residual`): a relay adds one more place for something to be paraphrased. Every user turn quoted below was checked against the coordinating session's own transcript and is reproduced exactly as sent, including typos, rather than cleaned up.

**`$environment_caveat`** - Both subagents ran as Task-tool agents launched from a session whose global CLAUDE.md and project memory index belong to this same product. Unlike run b's later checkouts, no separate `claude -p` process was used to rule out inherited context, and neither subagent was asked to declare whether it relied on outside knowledge. Take `checked` on these two observations as good evidence the agent read the repository in front of it, not as proof it was a total stranger to the product.

## The conversations

### 1. `A1` against repo:hagopj13/node-express-boilerplate (pre-adoption base)

**Mode:** full-loop | **Verdict:** partial

_No turn trace - this observation records a single exchange only._

**Where it ended up:** 15 commits on a scoped branch (`standards/adopt-repository-standards`), nothing pushed - `git remote set-url --push origin` was pointed at a non-existent remote before the subagent ever ran, and `git status` on the real `origin` confirms no ref changed. Wave 0 (interview, then `.standards-version` and a 74-line backlog written from the owner's own declared profile: `scale`, Layer 1 only, full alignment done in waves) and Wave 1 (`PRODUCT.md` and `personas.md` reconstructed from the generator's own CLI entry point and role definitions, not invented) are complete. Wave 2 - all eight foundational ADRs - is complete, and three of the eight were revised a second time after the owner was asked directly whether the AI's first-draft judgment call was actually right: domain boundaries flipped from 'accept the flat layout' to 'migrate to capability slices' (tracked as its own story, S32, not folded silently into the ADR); the security-baseline ADR's neutral framing of unrestricted CORS was overturned to 'this is a gap that needs fixing' (S33); the testing-strategy ADR's missing coverage threshold was recorded as a genuinely open, unanswered question rather than a number invented to fill the field. Waves 3-6 (specs, the backlog itself as a reviewable artifact, guard/structure work, suggested drift stories) were never started - the owner redirected to other priorities before reaching them, so this observation is scored on what ran, not on the six-wave plan it never finished.

**Where a person would give up:** Not in what the agent asked - in what the relay failed to surface. After the Wave-1 authorization was relayed ('yes, thats exacly right' / 'good, lets do as you suggest, phase by phase'), the subagent went silent for roughly an hour with zero new commits. A `SendMessage` resume reported success ('resumed from transcript in the background') while, checked directly against the subagent's own transcript file, nothing had actually resumed - the last entry was the same message already relayed, unchanged. A real user watching only the tool's own status line has no way to distinguish 'still thinking' from 'silently dead' at that point; the fix here was launching a fresh agent with recovered context rather than trusting a second blind resume.

**Why this verdict:** Every revision is independently checkable on the branch. Commit `a46be0e` records the owner's exact words on domain boundaries ('migrate all the way, not a partial or permanent exception') and adds S32 as the actual migration story rather than deciding the refactor inside the ADR. Commit `148aa2b` records the CORS reversal the same way. Commit `0365f74` records the coverage answer verbatim - 'no blanket minimum should be forced, business-logic coverage is what would actually matter, but business logic is not precisely defined yet' - rather than sharpening it into a policy nobody stated. The branching ADR (`d3b8673`) is the sharpest asked/checked evidence the round produced: going into Wave 2, this round's own working notes flagged 'proposing the standard's trunk-based default' as a likely case of the agent inventing policy, but the actual commit instead ran `git log --merges` against the real repository and recorded merge-commit PR integration as a *verified fact*, filing only the genuinely new gap - no release automation - as backlog story S31 rather than deciding one. Four of the eight ADRs (repo topology, datastore, API contract, authn/authz) are pure recovery from config files and code, nothing invented in them; the other four hit a real gap and asked before deciding, which is the exact line this round exists to find.
